steps.say: Gold adds compounding: the same percentage applied several times. First the yearly multiplier for a 10% increase.
steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

steps.say: It runs for 3 years, so raise the multiplier to the power 3.
Multiply the starting amount by this single factor.
Check the interest earned looks right for 3 years.
steps.done: £662 interest on £2000 over 3 years at 10% compound. The power did the work: that is the gold move.

steps.say: Bronze is one percentage change, done with a multiplier. This is an increase of 15%, so add 0.15 to 1.
steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

steps.say: Now multiply the original amount by it.
Read the answer back to be sure.
steps.hint: Subtract the original from the new price.

steps.say: And that increase should be 15% of 80.
steps.done: 12 matches, so £92 is right. That is the whole bronze move.

silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: Silver often works backwards. £96 is the price AFTER a 20% increase, so it is the original times the multiplier. Find that multiplier.
steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

steps.say: To undo the increase, divide instead of multiply.
steps.hint: Divide the final price by the multiplier.

steps.say: Read it back: the increase of 20% on £80.
steps.done: £80 + £16 = £96, so £80 is the original. Divide by the multiplier, never subtract from £96.

silver.display: A coat costs £96 after a 20% increase. Find the original price.

steps.say: No formulas yet. A £40 coat has 25% off. A quarter of £40 is £10.
That is the whole idea. Taking 25% off is the same as keeping 75%, and 75% as a decimal is 0.75, so £40 × 0.75 = £30 in one step. That 0.75 is called the multiplier.

steps.pre: 20% of £30 is £6, so you now pay 30 − 6 = £
steps.say: Now the twist. At the till you get a loyalty 20% off the £30 as well. A fifth of £30 is £6.

Two cuts did NOT make 45% off (that would leave £22). Each cut comes off a smaller price, so they stack: \(£40 \times 0.75 \times 0.80 = £24\). Multiplying multipliers together like this is all compound change is.

steps: Increase by r%: multiply by (1 + r/100). Decrease by r%: multiply by (1 − r/100).
Compound over n periods: Final = Original × (multiplier) to the power n.
Reverse: divide the final amount by the multiplier to find the original.
method_card.title: Percentages & Compound Change
method_card.content:
Percentage change: Multiply by a multiplier. Increase by 15% → ×1.15. Decrease by 20% → ×0.80.

Reverse percentages: If the result AFTER a change is known, divide by the multiplier to find the original.

Compound change: \(\text{Final} = \text{Original} \times (\text{multiplier})^n\) where \(n\) is the number of years/periods.

steps: The same percentage is applied every year, so raise the multiplier to a power: \(\text{Final} = \text{Original} \times (\text{multiplier})^n\).
Two 10% rises are NOT one 20% rise: each year acts on the new amount, so always use the power, never repeated addition.
Working backwards? Divide the final amount by \((\text{multiplier})^n\). To find how many years, apply the multiplier one year at a time until you pass the target.
gold.title: Gold: compound change over several years

steps: A single increase or decrease. Turn the percentage into a multiplier: an increase of \(r\%\) is \(1 + \frac{r}{100}\), a decrease is \(1 - \frac{r}{100}\).
Multiply the original amount by the multiplier. A 25% rise uses 1.25; a 30% fall uses 0.70.
Check by finding the change on its own: it should equal that percentage of the original.
bronze.title: Bronze: one percentage change

steps: Read the words to pick the multiplier: VAT of 20% or growth of 5% is an increase (1.20, 1.05); depreciation or a reduction is a decrease (0.90).
Multiply the starting amount by it. For simple interest, find one year's interest then multiply by the number of years.
To reverse a change, the amount you are given is the original already multiplied, so divide by the multiplier to get back.
silver.title: Silver: single-step problems and working backwards

example.question: After a 15% increase a phone costs £69. Find the original price.

gold.display: £3000 invested at 4% compound interest for 2 years. Find the final amount to 2 d.p.

guided_steps.say: Compound interest is a repeated increase. First the yearly multiplier for 4%.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: It runs for 2 years, so raise the multiplier to the power 2.
Now multiply the starting amount by this single factor.
Check the interest looks right for 2 years.
guided_steps.done: £244.80 interest on £3000 at 4% compound. So £3244.80 is right.

misconceptions.message: £3240 uses simple interest, adding 4% of £3000 twice. Compound multiplies each year: 3000 × 1.04² = £3244.80.

gold.hint: Multiply 15000 by 0.88 cubed, then round to the nearest pound.
gold.display: A car worth £15000 depreciates 12% per year. Value after 3 years? Round to nearest £.

guided_steps.say: Depreciation is a repeated decrease. First the yearly multiplier for 12%.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.12.

guided_steps.say: Over 3 years, raise the multiplier to the power 3.
Multiply the starting value by this factor.
The question asks for the nearest pound.
guided_steps.done: £10222 left after 3 years of 12% depreciation. That matches.

misconceptions.message: £9600 takes off 36% (12% × 3) in one go. Depreciation compounds: 15000 × 0.88³ = £10222.

gold.display: After 2 years of 5% compound interest, an account has £1102.50. Find the original amount.

guided_steps.say: A reverse compound problem. The final amount is the original times 1.05, twice over. First the yearly multiplier.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: Two years means the total factor is 1.05 squared.
Undo it by dividing the final amount by this factor.
Check by going forwards.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £1102.50, so the original was £1000.

misconceptions.message: Dividing by 1.05 once undoes only one year. Two years needs 1.05²: 1102.50 ÷ 1.1025 = £1000.

gold.hint: Apply the 0.97 multiplier one year at a time until the total first drops below 7000.
gold.display: A population of 8000 decreases by 3% per year. After how many whole years is it first below 7000? (Enter the number of years.)

guided_steps.say: The population loses 3% each year, so it multiplies by 0.97 every year. Test one year at a time.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.03.

guided_steps.say: Work out year 4 first. Is it still above 7000?
7082 is still above 7000, so go one more year.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the year-4 value by 0.97 once more.

guided_steps.pre: The first whole year below 7000 is year
guided_steps.say: Year 5 is the first below 7000.
guided_steps.done: Year 4 = 7082 (above), year 5 = 6870 (below). So 5 years.
guided_steps.hint: Year 4 was above, year 5 is below.

misconceptions.message: After 4 years the population is 7082, still above 7000. After 5 years it is 6870, the first year below 7000. The answer is 5 years, not 4.

gold.hint: Find the total with 1.06 squared, then subtract the original to get the interest.
gold.display: £500 earns 6% compound interest. How much interest (not total) after 2 years? To 2 d.p.

guided_steps.say: Compound interest. First the yearly multiplier for 6%.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: Two years, so raise the multiplier to the power 2.
Find the total amount first.
The question wants the interest, not the total, so subtract the starting amount.
guided_steps.done: £61.80 interest on £500 at 6% compound over 2 years. That matches.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from the total.

misconceptions.message: £561.80 is the total amount. The question asks for the interest only: 561.80 − 500 = £61.80.
£60 is simple interest, 6% of £500 twice. Compound gives a total of £561.80, so the interest is £61.80.

bronze.hint: Increase means multiply by 1.10 (or find 10% and add it on).

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. An increase of 10% keeps the whole amount and adds a tenth, so add 0.10 to 1.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.1.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the increase on its own should be 10% of 200.
guided_steps.done: 20 is 10% of 200. So £220 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from your new total.

misconceptions.message: £20 is only 10% of £200, the increase by itself. Add it back on: 200 + 20 = £220. Or multiply by 1.10 in one step.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. A decrease of 20% keeps 80% of the amount, so take 0.20 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.2.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the amount lost should be 20% of 150.
guided_steps.done: 30 is 20% of 150. So £120 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract your answer from the original.

misconceptions.message: £30 is only 20% of £150, the amount taken off. Subtract it: 150 − 30 = £120. Or multiply by 0.80 in one step.

bronze.hint: 25% is a quarter, so divide by 4.

guided_steps.say: 25% means 25 out of 100, which is a quarter.
Multiply 60 by the decimal to find the part.
Four lots of 25% should rebuild the whole 60.
guided_steps.done: Four 15s make 60, so 15 is exactly a quarter of 60.

misconceptions.message: £45 is £60 with 25% taken off. The question asks for 25% OF £60, which is just 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

bronze.display: A shirt costs £40. It is reduced by 10%. What is the sale price?

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. Reduced by 10% leaves 90% of the price, so take 0.10 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.1.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original price by the multiplier.
Check: the discount should be 10% of 40.
guided_steps.done: 4 is 10% of 40. So £36 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the sale price from the original.

misconceptions.message: £4 is the discount (10% of £40), not the price you pay. Take it off: 40 − 4 = £36. Or multiply by 0.90 in one step.

bronze.display: What multiplier represents an increase of 5%?

guided_steps.say: An increase keeps the whole original (100%) and adds the extra. First write 5% as a decimal.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100: move the point two places.

guided_steps.say: An increase adds this to 1, the 100% you keep.
Check by reading it back: a multiplier of 1.05 keeps 100% and adds how much?
guided_steps.done: 5% extra, exactly the increase asked for. So 1.05 is right.

misconceptions.message: 0.05 is 5% written as a decimal, the extra part only. A multiplier keeps the whole 1 and adds it: 1 + 0.05 = 1.05.

bronze.hint: A decrease takes away from 1: 1 minus 0.30.
bronze.display: What multiplier represents a decrease of 30%?

guided_steps.say: A decrease keeps what is left after taking the percentage away. First write 30% as a decimal.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100: move the point two places.

guided_steps.say: A decrease takes this off 1, the 100% you started with.
Check: how much has been taken off?
guided_steps.done: 30% taken off, exactly the decrease asked for. So 0.7 is right.

misconceptions.message: 0.3 is 30% written as a decimal, the part removed. A decrease keeps what is left: 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

bronze.hint: Divide the money change by the ORIGINAL price, then multiply by 100.
bronze.display: A price increases from £50 to £60. What is the percentage increase?

guided_steps.say: Percentage change compares the change to what you started with. First find the actual change.
Now write the change as a fraction of the original price, not the new one.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the change by the ORIGINAL, 50.

guided_steps.say: Turn the decimal into a percentage.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply by 100 to make a percentage.

guided_steps.say: Check forwards: a 20% increase on 50 should land on 60.
guided_steps.done: 50 rises to 60, so 20% is right.

misconceptions.message: £10 is the money increase, not the percentage. Divide by the original and multiply by 100: 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%.
Dividing by £60, the new price, gives 16.7%. Percentage change divides by the ORIGINAL: 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. An increase of 50% adds 0.5 to 1.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.5.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the increase should be 50% of 300.
guided_steps.done: 150 is 50% of 300. So 450 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from your new value.

misconceptions.message: 150 is only the increase (50% of 300), not the new total. Add it back on: 300 + 150 = 450. Or multiply by 1.5 in one step.

silver.display: A TV costs £510 after a 15% increase. Find the original price.

guided_steps.say: A reverse percentage. £510 is the price AFTER a 15% increase, so it is the original times the multiplier. Find that multiplier first.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: To undo the increase, divide the final price by the multiplier. Round to 2 d.p.
Check by going forwards: the original plus 15% should return £510.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £510, so £443.48 is right.

misconceptions.message: Taking 15% off £510 gives £433.50, but the 15% was added to the ORIGINAL, not to £510. Divide instead: 510 ÷ 1.15 = £443.48.

silver.hint: Simple interest: one year's interest, then multiply by the number of years.
silver.display: £1000 earns 5% simple interest per year. How much interest after 3 years?

guided_steps.say: Simple interest adds the same amount each year. First find one year's interest.
Simple interest does not compound, so just multiply by the number of years.

guided_steps.pre: Check the total in the account: 1000 + 150 = £
guided_steps.say: Read it back: the account holds the original plus the interest.
guided_steps.done: £150 interest sits on top of the £1000. So £150 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add the interest to the start.

misconceptions.message: £50 is one year's interest. Simple interest repeats it: 50 × 3 = £150.
£1150 is the total in the account. The question asks for the interest only: 1150 − 1000 = £150.

silver.display: A car worth £12000 depreciates by 10% per year. What is it worth after 1 year?

guided_steps.say: Depreciation is a decrease. First the multiplier for losing 10%.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.1.

guided_steps.say: Multiply the current value by the multiplier.
Check: the value lost should be 10% of 12000.

misconceptions.message: £1200 is the fall in value (10% of 12000), not what the car is worth. Take it off: 12000 − 1200 = £10800.

silver.display: After a 20% reduction, a coat costs £56. Find the original price.

guided_steps.say: A reverse percentage. £56 is the price AFTER a 20% reduction, so it is the original times 0.80. Find that multiplier first.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1.

guided_steps.say: To undo the reduction, divide the final price by the multiplier.
Check by going forwards: the original minus 20% should return £56.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £56, so £70 is right.

misconceptions.message: Adding 20% to £56 gives £67.20, but the 20% came off the ORIGINAL price. Divide instead: 56 ÷ 0.80 = £70.

silver.display: A population of 5000 increases by 2% each year. What is it after 1 year?

guided_steps.say: Growth is an increase. First the multiplier for a 2% rise.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.02.

guided_steps.say: Multiply the starting population by the multiplier.
Check: the rise should be 2% of 5000.
guided_steps.done: 100 is 2% of 5000. So 5100 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the start from your answer.

misconceptions.message: 100 is the rise (2% of 5000), not the new population. Add it on: 5000 + 100 = 5100.

silver.display: VAT is 20%. A laptop costs £480 before VAT. What is the price including VAT?

guided_steps.say: Adding VAT is an increase. First the multiplier for adding 20%.
Multiply the price before VAT by the multiplier.
Check: the VAT added should be 20% of 480.
guided_steps.done: 96 is 20% of 480. So £576 is right.

misconceptions.message: £96 is the VAT (20% of 480), not the total. Add it on: 480 + 96 = £576.

silver.hint: Divide the money drop by the ORIGINAL price, then multiply by 100.
silver.display: A price drops from £80 to £64. What is the percentage decrease?

guided_steps.say: Percentage change compares the drop to what you started with. First find the actual drop.
Write the drop as a fraction of the original price, not the new one.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the drop by the ORIGINAL, 80.

guided_steps.say: Turn the decimal into a percentage.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply by 100 to make a percentage.

guided_steps.say: Check forwards: a 20% decrease on 80 should land on 64.
guided_steps.done: 80 falls to 64, so 20% is right.

misconceptions.message: 16 is the money drop, not the percentage. Divide by the original and multiply by 100: 16 ÷ 80 × 100 = 20%.
Dividing by £64, the new price, gives 25%. Percentage change divides by the ORIGINAL: 16 ÷ 80 × 100 = 20%.

problem_bank.gold_description: Compound change over several years, reverse compound, and how many years to reach a target.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One percentage increase or decrease, done in your head with a multiplier.
problem_bank.silver_description: Single-step money problems: a percentage change in a real context, or working backwards to an original.

worked_examples.question: A jacket costs £68 after a 15% discount. Find the original price.
£2000 invested at 4% compound interest for 3 years. Find the final amount.
